full_judgment: 21. Next to consider is whether the High Court Division has failed to consider the relevant evidence, law and the rules applicable to the case properly. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that High Court Division misread the service records of the plaintiff and the rules and law bearing upon the same. It failed to consider the relevant evidence in their true legal perspective. It appears that the High Court Division laboured under a misconception that the service book was interpolated by enhancing the age of the plaintiff, because in the bio-data Ext. Ga(1) filed at the time of his joining he recorded his date of birth as 28 February 1942. In reality this bio-data was submitted long 6 years after his joining the service. Besides, the conclusion arrived at by the High Court Division in respect of interpolation has been conjectural. The medical certificate dated 4 June 1963 refers to the educational certificate, the statement of the plaintiff himself and also appearance for recording his age as 30 years. The plaintiff himself signed the medical certificate and put his thumb impressions on the same date of 4 June 1963. On 11 June 1963 the plaintiff filed an application under his own signature to the Assistant Secretary of the Corporation for acceptance of the medical certificate. The service book of the plaintiff which was opened on 17 June 1963 and bears the signatures and thumb impressions of the plaintiff himself records his date of birth to be 4 June 1933 with reference to the medical certificate. Rule 9 of the Service Rules sets a bar to a change of the date of birth of the incumbent as recorded at the time of appointment. It is only on 15 July 1969 that the plaintiff had filed his new bio-data stating his date of birth to be 28 February 1942 which under Rule 9 was not acceptable.
